questions.q: What does the pipe operator (|) do?
options: Redirects a command's output into a file, overwriting it
Sends the standard output of the command on its left into the standard input of the command on its right
Runs two commands at the same time in the background
Combines stdout and stderr into one stream
questions.explain: A pipe connects one command's stdout directly to the next command's stdin, with no file created in between.

questions.q: You run `echo "line one" > notes.txt` and then `echo "line two" > notes.txt`. What ends up in notes.txt?
options: Only 'line two', because > overwrites the file each time
Only 'line one', because the file can't be reopened
An error, because the file already exists
questions.explain: > overwrites the target file every time it's used. To add a new line without erasing the old ones, you need >> instead.

questions.q: A script prints a warning to stderr that you want captured in a log file along with its normal output. Which redirection does that?
questions.explain: Redirecting stdout to the file first, then using 2>&1 to merge stderr into that same destination, captures both streams in one file.

questions.q: What is the purpose of redirecting output to /dev/null?
options: It saves the output to a hidden backup file
It discards the output entirely — nothing is kept anywhere
It sends the output to the system log instead of the terminal
It pipes the output into the next command automatically
questions.explain: /dev/null is a special file that silently discards anything written to it, which is useful when you want output gone, not saved.

questions.q: Which file descriptor number corresponds to standard error?
questions.explain: File descriptor 0 is stdin, 1 is stdout, and 2 is stderr — the number used in redirections like 2> and 2>&1.
